content.title: About
content.content: Raw apricots are juicy fruits of the apricot tree (Prunus armeniaca) that grow in temperate to warm regions worldwide. They have a sweet‑tart flavor, aromatic flesh, and a delicate velvety skin.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Apricots belong to the Rosaceae family and are closely related to peaches, plums, and cherries.
High β‑carotene content makes them an excellent source of provitamin A.
In ancient cultures the apricot symbolized longevity and fertility.
Dried apricots have been used in traditional medicine to aid digestion.
The skin is rich in antioxidants, though it may contain trace amounts of cyanogenic glycosides.

items.title: Rich in vitamin A
items.content: β‑carotene converts to vitamin A, supporting vision and immune function.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C enhances antioxidant protection and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and helps maintain satiety.

items.title: Potassium and magnesium
items.content: These minerals aid normal blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: Low‑calorie fruit
items.content: Moderate natural sugar makes apricots a good choice for calorie‑conscious diets.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to apricots.

items.title: Cyanogenic glycosides
items.content: The skin and pit contain small amounts of toxic compounds; they should not be consumed in large quantities.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: People with diabetes should monitor portion size due to natural sugars.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Raw apricots can be eaten as a snack, added to salads, yogurts, cereals, baked goods, or made into sauces. Remove the pit before consumption.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store apricots in the refrigerator’s fruit drawer, in a plastic container or bag. At room temperature they ripen quickly, so use within 2–3 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Bloody Mary is a ready‑to‑mix blend for making the classic Bloody Mary cocktail, containing tomato juice, spices, flavorings, and sometimes a pinch of salt. It is designed for quick and convenient preparation at home.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The Bloody Mary cocktail originated in the United States in the 1920s and quickly became popular as a "hair of the dog" drink.
Tomato juice gives the drink its rich flavor and bright red color, while spices like Worcestershire sauce, Tabasco, and black pepper provide characteristic heat.
Bloody Mary is often served with celery stalks, olives, pickles, or shrimp as garnish.
The drink is believed to help relieve hangovers thanks to the vitamins and antioxidants in tomatoes.
Various countries have their own twists, adding horseradish, soy sauce, or even bacon.

items.title: Rich in lycopene
items.content: Tomato juice is a good source of lycopene, a powerful antioxidant that supports heart health and may reduce the risk of certain cancers.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains vitamin B6 and folate (B9), important for metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Electrolytes
items.content: Salt and tomato juice provide sodium and potassium, helping maintain fluid balance.

items.title: Anti‑inflammatory compounds
items.content: Spices such as black pepper and Worcestershire sauce contain compounds with anti‑inflammatory effects.

items.title: Digestive aid
items.content: Tomato juice and spices stimulate gastric secretions, aiding digestion.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: The added salt can be problematic for people with hypertension; portion control is recommended.

items.title: Spicy flavor
items.content: Tabasco and Worcestershire sauce make the drink very hot, which may irritate sensitive stomachs.

items.title: Allergy to ingredients
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to components like soy sauce or anchovies found in Worcestershire sauce.

items.title: Acidity of tomato juice
items.content: The acidic nature can exacerbate heartburn in those with gastritis or reflux.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Mix 200 ml of the blend with 50 ml of vodka, add ice, and garnish with a celery stalk, olive, or lemon wedge. Optional additions include lime juice, horseradish, or bacon for variations.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the packet in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep it refrigerated and use within 3–4 days. Discard if the smell or taste changes.

coffee-brewed-blend-of-regular-and-decaf.title: Coffee, brewed, blend of regular and decaffeinated

content.title: About
content.content: Coffee is a beverage made from roasted and ground seeds of the coffee plant. This version is a blend of regular and decaffeinated coffee, offering the full aroma and flavor with reduced caffeine content.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Blends of regular and decaf coffee are popular in offices where sustained alertness is needed without strong stimulation.
Decaffeinated coffee is produced either by removing caffeine from green beans or by using naturally low‑caffeine varieties.
The aromatic profile of the blend can be more balanced, as decaf softens the bitterness of regular coffee.
Coffee is the second most traded commodity in the world after oil.
There are over 100 species of coffee plants, but commercially only Arabica and Robusta are widely cultivated.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Coffee is rich in polyphenols that help combat free radicals and may lower the risk of certain chronic diseases.

items.title: Cognitive support
items.content: Moderate coffee consumption is linked to improved attention, memory, and reaction time.

items.title: Reduced risk of type 2 diabetes
items.content: Studies suggest regular coffee drinking can decrease the likelihood of developing diabetes.

items.title: Liver protection
items.content: Coffee consumption is associated with a lower risk of cirrhosis and some liver cancers.

items.title: Metabolism boost
items.content: Caffeine speeds up metabolism, which can aid weight management.

items.title: Caffeine sensitivity
items.content: Some individuals may experience anxiety, insomnia, or rapid heartbeat even with small amounts of caffeine.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Coffee can irritate the stomach in people with gastritis or acid reflux.

items.title: Drug interactions
items.content: Caffeine may amplify the effects of certain stimulants and diminish the efficacy of some sedatives.

items.title: Pregnancy
items.content: Pregnant women are advised to limit caffeine intake to 200 mg per day.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use 1‑2 teaspoons of ground coffee per 180‑200 ml of hot water (90‑95 °C) and steep for 3‑5 minutes. The blend works well for drip, French press, or espresso machines. Add milk, cream, or plant‑based alternatives if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store ground coffee in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. Keep it away from air, moisture, and light to preserve aroma and flavor. Shelf life is about 3‑6 months after opening.

content.title: About
content.content: A cream puff (eclair) is a small choux pastry filled with custard or whipped cream and topped with icing. This version is made with reduced fat, using less butter and low‑fat milk, while preserving the light, airy texture and delicate flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The classic French eclair gets its name from the lightning‑fast way it disappears at bakeries.
Choux pastry is leavened by steam, not yeast, giving it a hollow interior perfect for filling.
Reduced‑fat recipes replace part of the butter with vegetable oil and use skimmed milk in the cream.
Eclairs are a popular party treat because they can be easily glazed in many colors.
In Russia, cream‑filled pastries are often enjoyed with fruit jams or chocolate glaze.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: Eggs in the choux dough provide high‑quality protein essential for muscle maintenance.

items.title: Contains calcium
items.content: Low‑fat milk in the filling supplies calcium for bone health.

items.title: Lower saturated fat
items.content: Reducing butter cuts saturated fat, supporting heart‑friendly nutrition.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs and dairy contribute B2, B12 and folate, which aid energy metabolism.

items.title: Moderate sugar level
items.content: The recipe uses a modest amount of sugar, helping to keep blood‑glucose spikes in check.

items.title: Egg and milk allergy
items.content: People allergic to eggs or dairy should avoid this product.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Despite reduced fat, the pastry still contains sugar, so diabetics should monitor portions.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Lower fat reduces calories, but a single puff can still be energy‑dense.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: The wheat flour base contains gluten, making it unsuitable for those with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Eat cream puffs by hand as a dessert or snack. Pair them with fresh berries, fruit sauce, or a cup of tea. For extra indulgence, drizzle a light glaze on top.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep puffs in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 days. For longer freshness, refrigerate for up to 5 days. Allow them to come to room temperature before serving.

ham-or-pork-and-rice-no-sauce.title: Ham or pork and rice, no sauce

content.title: About
content.content: The dish consists of boiled rice served with pieces of ham or boiled/fried pork without any sauce. It is a simple, hearty and nutritious meal, popular in cafeterias and home kitchens, especially during colder months.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Rice is one of the most consumed grains worldwide, and its combination with meat provides a complete amino‑acid profile.
Traditionally in Russia the dish was prepared in winter when quick energy and warmth were needed.
Ham, as a smoked meat, can be stored longer without refrigeration, making it convenient for field conditions.
The meal is often served in a “tray” portion in school canteens, simplifying distribution.
The lack of sauce makes the dish less calorie‑dense while preserving the natural flavors of meat and rice.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Meat provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Rice supplies complex carbohydrates that release energy gradually.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Pork and ham contain vitamin B12, niacin and riboflavin, supporting the nervous system.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The dish offers iron, zinc and phosphorus, important for blood formation and bones.

items.title: Low sugar content
items.content: Without sauce, added sugars are minimal.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Ham is often salty; people with hypertension should limit portion size.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Pork can be fatty; choose lean cuts or trim excess fat.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Some hams contain nitrites; opt for products without additives when possible.

items.title: Gluten sensitivity
items.content: If rice is cooked with soy sauce, it may trigger reactions in gluten‑sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot; you can add fresh vegetables or herbs for extra flavor. A pinch of black pepper or a squeeze of lemon juice is optional.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared meal in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Reheat thoroughly to a rolling boil to prevent bacterial growth.

content.title: About
content.content: Lemon juice 100 % is pure juice extracted from ripe lemons, pasteurized and packaged in glass or metal containers. It retains the characteristic tart flavor, aroma, and most of the vitamins, especially vitamin C.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Lemons are among the oldest cultivated citrus fruits, with cultivation dating back over 2,500 years in Southeast Asia.
When pasteurized at low temperature and stored in dark bottles, the juice preserves almost all of its nutrients.
Lemon juice is widely used as a natural preservative in cooking because of its high acidity (pH ≈ 2.5).
In the United States, more than 30 % of all canned juices are lemon juice, often used in beverages and sauces.
Beyond culinary uses, lemon juice can help remove stains and odors around the house.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: One cup (250 ml) of lemon juice provides over 150 % of the daily recommended vitamin C, supporting immunity and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Flavonoids and citric acid act as antioxidants, helping neutralize free radicals and protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Aids digestion
items.content: The acidity stimulates gastric juice production, improving food breakdown and nutrient absorption.

items.title: May reduce kidney stone risk
items.content: Citrate present in lemons can help prevent the formation of calcium oxalate stones.

items.title: Hydration and electrolytes
items.content: Lemon juice contains small amounts of potassium and magnesium, contributing to fluid‑electrolyte balance.

items.title: Acid reflux
items.content: People with gastro‑esophageal reflux disease (GERD) may experience worsened heartburn from highly acidic juice.

items.title: Tooth enamel erosion
items.content: Frequent consumption of undiluted lemon juice can erode dental enamel due to its acidity.

items.title: Citrus allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may develop allergic reactions to lemons, manifesting as skin rash or swelling.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: Acidity can affect the absorption of certain drugs, such as iron supplements.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Lemon juice is used in drinks, marinades, sauces, baked goods, and desserts. It can be diluted in water, added to tea or cocktails, and used as a salad dressing. When drinking straight, it is advisable to dilute with water to lessen the acidity.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened containers in a cool, dark place. After opening, keep refrigerated and consume within 7‑10 days. Discard if the color changes, an off‑odor develops, or mold appears.

content.title: About
content.content: Boston lettuce is a crisp, light‑green leafy vegetable cultivated in the United States. It has a mild, slightly sweet flavor and firm yet tender leaves. Boston lettuce is commonly used in fresh salads, sandwiches, and as a garnish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Boston lettuce belongs to the Asteraceae family and is a variety of leaf lettuce.
It was named after the city of Boston, where it was first commercially developed in the early 20th century.
Its leaves are generally denser and less fragile than those of romaine or iceberg lettuce.
Boston lettuce is often grown in greenhouses, allowing year‑round production.
It is composed of more than 95 % water, making it an excellent source of hydration.

items.title: Rich in vitamin K
items.content: Boston lettuce provides a high amount of vitamin K, which is essential for blood clotting and bone health.

items.title: Source of folate
items.content: Folate supports normal cell division and is especially important during pregnancy.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: Its calorie content is very low, making it a great choice for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: The leaves contain carotenoids and vitamin C, which help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to leafy vegetables, including lettuce.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Raw lettuce can be contaminated with gut bacteria such as E. coli, so thorough washing is essential.

items.title: Pesticide residues
items.content: Conventional production may involve chemical pesticides; choosing organic or washing well reduces exposure.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Boston lettuce is typically eaten raw: in fresh salads, as part of sandwiches, in wraps, or as a side to meat dishes. Leaves can be torn by hand or sliced. For extra crispness, rinse them in cold water and spin dry in a salad spinner.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store Boston lettuce in the refrigerator in a slightly damp bag or a container with ventilation holes. Use within 3–5 days. Discard any leaves that become yellowed or limp.

content.title: About
content.content: A light homemade chocolate milk shake is made from skim milk, cocoa powder, a touch of honey or maple syrup, and ice. It has a smooth chocolate flavor, low calorie count, and works well as a breakfast or snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cocoa powder is rich in antioxidants that help fight free radicals.
Making the shake at home lets you control the amount of sugar, offering a healthier alternative to store‑bought versions.
A pinch of salt enhances the perception of sweetness without adding extra sugar.
The light version is often used in weight‑loss diets because of its low calorie density.
The shake can be prepared in a blender in 2‑3 minutes.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Cocoa contains flavonoids that support cardiovascular health and reduce inflammation.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Skim milk provides calcium essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Using non‑fat milk makes the shake suitable for low‑fat diet plans.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: The combination of milk carbohydrates and a small amount of sweetener quickly replenishes glycogen stores.

items.title: Mood improvement
items.content: Cocoa stimulates serotonin production, which can lift mood.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People with lactose intolerance or milk allergy should use plant‑based milk alternatives.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Excessive sweetener can raise the drink’s glycemic index.

items.title: Caffeine in cocoa
items.content: Cocoa may cause mild stimulation in some individuals, which might be undesirable before bedtime.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the shake chilled; you can top it with a dollop of low‑fat whipped cream or a sprinkle of dark chocolate shavings. It’s perfect for breakfast, post‑workout, or as a light dessert.

content.title: Storage
content.content: The shake is best enjoyed immediately. If needed, store it in a sealed container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Shake gently before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Italian pastry with cheese is a flaky dough filled with a savory cheese mixture, often enriched with herbs and spices. Baked until golden, it combines a crisp crust with a creamy, slightly salty cheese interior.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cheese pastries are popular in many Italian regions, where local cheeses such as mozzarella, parmesan, or gorgonzola are used.
The flaky dough, known as "pasta" in Italy, achieves its layers through repeated rolling and folding with butter.
Cheese fillings are frequently blended with eggs and cream to create a richer texture.
These pastries are traditionally served as an appetizer with wine or as part of a breakfast spread.
Some variations add dried fruits or nuts to the filling, offering a sweet‑savory contrast.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Cheese provides a good amount of calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: The cheese and eggs supply complete protein needed for tissue repair.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Cheeses, especially parmesan, are high in vitamins B2 and B12, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Healthy fats
items.content: Small amounts of mono‑ and polyunsaturated fats in cheese contribute to heart health.

items.title: Fiber from the dough
items.content: Using whole‑grain flour adds dietary fiber, aiding digestion.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Cheese contains lactose; those with intolerance should choose lactose‑free alternatives.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Cheeses can be salty, so individuals monitoring sodium intake should limit portions.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Flaky dough and cheese make the pastry energy‑dense; moderation is key for weight management.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People allergic to milk proteins may experience reactions when consuming.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pastry warm, cut into bite‑size pieces. It works well as a standalone snack, paired with a fresh salad, or as part of a brunch alongside fruit and a light wine.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 days. For longer storage, refrigerate up to 5 days or freeze for up to 1 month.

content.title: About
content.content: Peanut butter and chocolate spread is a ready‑to‑use paste that combines ground peanuts, cocoa butter, sugar and sometimes additives such as salt, vanilla or vegetable oils. The spread has a creamy texture, a sweet‑nutty flavor with chocolate notes, and is often used as a topping for bread, in desserts and baked goods.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The peanut‑chocolate combination is popular in the US and Europe as a quick energy snack.
Commercial versions first appeared in the 1970s when manufacturers began adding melted chocolate to classic peanut butter.
Cocoa butter content can range from 5 % to 20 % depending on the brand.
Some versions are fortified with probiotics or vitamins D and B12 for added benefit.
The spread is frequently used in sports nutrition because of its high protein and fast‑carb content.

items.title: Rich source of plant protein
items.content: Peanut butter provides about 25 g of protein per 100 g, helping to maintain muscle mass.

items.title: High energy density
items.content: The blend of fats and carbohydrates delivers quick energy, useful before workouts or as a snack.

items.title: Contains heart‑healthy monounsaturated fats
items.content: Most of the fat in peanut butter is monounsaturated, which supports cardiovascular health.

items.title: Source of magnesium and vitamin E
items.content: Peanuts are rich in magnesium, while chocolate contributes vitamin E, both antioxidants that protect cells.

items.title: Mood‑enhancing compounds
items.content: Cocoa butter contains phenylethylamine, which may promote the release of endorphins.

items.title: Peanut allergy
items.content: Peanut butter is a strong allergen; individuals with peanut allergy can experience severe reactions.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: The spread is calorie‑dense (about 550 kcal per 100 g), so portion control is important.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Sweetened versions may contain up to 30 g of sugar per 100 g, which is undesirable for diabetics or weight‑loss diets.

items.title: Trans fats in some brands
items.content: Certain manufacturers use partially hydrogenated oils, leading to trans‑fat formation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Spread can be used on toast, bagels, pancakes, added to smoothies, yogurt, oatmeal, or as a filling for cupcakes and cookies. For a thinner consistency, gently warm the paste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in an airtight jar in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, refrigeration is recommended to prevent fat oxidation. Discard if the spread develops a rancid smell or changes color.

content.title: About
content.content: Hard flavored pretzels are baked wheat‑flour snacks formed into the classic knot shape and baked until a crisp crust forms. After the first bake they are coated with salt and a variety of flavorings (cheese, onion, paprika, garlic, etc.) and baked again to lock in the taste.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pretzels have a medieval European origin; the modern hard pretzel evolved from the traditional German "Brezel".
Flavorings are applied after the initial bake and the pretzel is finished with a second bake to set the seasoning.
The hard texture makes pretzels ideal for long‑term storage and transport.
In the United States more than 2 billion servings of pretzels are consumed each year.
The iconic knot shape was historically used as a good‑luck symbol by bakers.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Pretzels provide starch that supplies steady energy and helps keep you feeling full.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Wheat flour contributes a modest amount of iron, essential for oxygen transport.

items.title: Vitamin B6 content
items.content: Vitamin B6 supports protein metabolism and nervous‑system function.

items.title: Low in added sugar
items.content: Unlike many sweet snacks, hard pretzels typically contain little to no added sugar.

items.title: Fiber in whole‑grain versions
items.content: Whole‑grain pretzels add dietary fiber that aids digestion.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Pretzels made from wheat flour can trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: The salty coating can contribute to excess sodium intake, which may be a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Calorie density
items.content: The hard, dense texture means a small serving can contain a notable number of calories.

items.title: Choking hazard
items.content: Hard, crunchy pieces may pose a choking risk for young children.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy pretzels as a standalone snack, pair them with cheese, mustard, hummus, or dip sauces. They also add a crunchy element to salads, charcuterie boards, and snack mixes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep pretzels in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For extended freshness, store them in the refrigerator to maintain their crispness.

content.title: About
content.content: Canned strawberries are whole strawberry berries that have been heat‑processed and sealed in glass or metal jars with syrup or their own juice. The berries retain their sweet flavor and much of the vitamins and minerals typical of fresh strawberries.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Strawberries are one of the few berries that contain a notable amount of vitamin C.
Canning allows strawberries to be stored for several years without losing taste.
The syrup used for canning is usually a simple sugar‑water solution, sometimes with added citric acid to preserve colour.
In the United States more than 200,000 tons of canned strawberries are produced each year.
Strawberries belong to the rose family, along with apples, pears and cherries.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and aids collagen synthesis, important for skin and blood vessels.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Flavonoids and anthocyanins in strawberries help combat free radicals, reducing the risk of chronic diseases.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Strawberries provide dietary fiber that promotes regular bowel movements.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and supports heart function.

items.title: Low‑calorie snack
items.content: One typical jar (about 200 g) contains roughly 70 kcal, making it a convenient light snack.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: The syrup often contains added sugar, which may be problematic for people with diabetes or those watching their weight.

items.title: Strawberry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to strawberries, ranging from skin rashes to swelling.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Certain brands may use preservatives such as potassium sorbate to extend shelf life.

items.title: Citric acid
items.content: Citric acid is sometimes added to maintain bright colour, but in large amounts it can irritate the stomach.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Canned strawberries can be eaten straight from the jar, added to yogurt, oatmeal, desserts, baked goods, or used in sauces for meat dishes. If you are monitoring sugar intake, drain the syrup before use.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened jars in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep the jar refrigerated and consume within 3–5 days. Discard if mold appears or the smell becomes off.
